title: Scan like Messi
author: Thahmina Begum
summary: Thahmina Begum, writing a bi-weekly T&L bulletin for staff at Community Schools Trust, uses footballer Lionel Messi's high scan rate as an analogy for expert teachers who scan the room more and more evenly. Her diagnosis is a common error in the first weeks of term: teachers call for SLANT to deliver an explanation but fail to correct students who slip out of it seconds later. She offers five linked moves: front-load the means of participation, be seen looking, notice small signs of drift, issue a calm reminder, and re-engage the student with a task or cold call. The piece grounds scanning in research on situation awareness and professional vision as looking, noticing and responding. She ends by tying habit formation, and the so-called valley of disappointment, to the need to consistently disrupt deviation from a routine.
points: Expert teachers scan more often and more evenly, and that scanning is linked to more accurate judgements about pupils.
Front-loading the means of participation, telling students how to participate before telling them what to do, prevents many slips out of SLANT.
Be Seen Looking techniques such as the Invisible Column, the Tiptoes and the Sprinkler make scanning visible and less predictable.
Effective scanning has three linked acts, looking, noticing and responding, and teachers who skip the last two end up with an expectation that is stated but inconsistently enforced.
A correction should be small but certain, followed by re-engagement through a question and a reward so students return to thinking and not just posture.
quotes: Better teachers scan more – and, like Messi, that scanning gives them better information to act on.
Remember the purpose of using SLANT: we use it to ensure 100% attention because we know that what we attend to, we think about. What we think about, we are more likely to learn.
So if we believe SLANT is important at the start of an explanation, it has to matter 30 seconds into it too.
As Boxer explains, FLMOP is a behavioural nudge. It makes the behaviour we want more likely before we have to correct the behaviour we don’t.
Lemov’s point is that it isn’t enough to look; students need to see you looking.
Those of us who have not established SLANT as a habit of attention can often miss the latter 2 acts. Without them, SLANT quickly becomes an expectation that is stated but inconsistently enforced.
Every time we notice a student come out of SLANT and choose not to correct it, we make the expectation a little less certain.
A routine only becomes a habit when deviation from it is consistently disrupted.
